description_full: Samsonite Group S.A. engages in the design, manufacture, sourcing, and distribution of luggage, business and computer bags, outdoor and casual bags, and travel accessories in Asia, North America, Europe, and Latin America. The company sells its products under the Samsonite, Tumi, American Tourister, Gregory, High Sierra, Kamiliant, Saxoline, Secret, Lipault, and Hartmann brands, as well as other owned and licensed brand names. It distributes its products through wholesale distribution channels, as well as through company-operated retail stores and e-commerce. The company was formerly known as Samsonite International S.A. and changed its name to Samsonite Group S.A. in January 2025. Samsonite Group S.A. was founded in 1910 and is headquartered in Luxembourg, Luxembourg.
ceo_bio: Mr. Kyle Francis Gendreau CPA | CEO & Executive Director | Age 55 | Compensation: $3.2M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 11K people. Revenue per employee of $308K ranks in the below the sector median among Consumer Cyclical peers. Each employee generates $36K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $811 per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 10× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity).
financial_summary: SAMSONITE GROUP S A is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $2.5B market cap on $3.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 15% against a 7% cost of capital, a 8-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 59% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $412M in free cash flow — roughly 12 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.75× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.2× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.1×.

Management returns a meaningful 7.6% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (1.8) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent

Consumer demand is fundamentally cyclical — a recession compresses both unit volume and pricing power, and operating leverage cuts both ways.
E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

sect: Its 15% operating margin runs 8pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (8%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.88x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 15% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 35% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 40% and a beta of 0.75, it is more defensive than the market.
Trading is thin (about $60K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 74% in the 2020 crash and 30% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 62% below its DCF fair value of $23.74, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 9%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $17.38 to $32.87 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 9.8 vs 19.3, EV/EBITDA 7.1 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 6.0 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 16.6% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 13.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 12.2% annual cash-flow growth, 13pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 15% clears the cost of capital of 7.0% by 8pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.13).
It runs a 59% gross margin and converts 12% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.75x.
ROE of 18% is amplified by 3.2x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.2x net debt to EBITDA ($649.3M of cash against $2.4B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 4.1x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.78 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.7% over 3 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 0%.
It returns 7.6% a year to shareholders (1.5% in buybacks and 5.6% in dividends).
people: With about 11,350 employees, each generates about $308K of revenue, 0.8x the Consumer Cyclical median.
That works out to $36K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.2M (10x revenue per employee).
